blocks.text: 25. Instrument, Drum and Effect Racks
blocks.raw_html: 25. Instrument, Drum and Effect Racks

blocks.text: A Rack is a flexible tool for working with effects, plug-ins and instruments in a track’s device chain. Racks can be used to build complex signal processors, dynamic performance instruments, stacked synthesizers and more. Yet they also streamline your device chain by bringing together your most essential controls. While Racks excel at handling multiple devices, they can extend the abilities of even a single device by defining new control relationships between its parameters.

heading_context.text: 25.1.1 Signal Flow and Parallel Device Chains

blocks.text: In any of Live’s tracks, devices are connected serially in a device chain, passing their signals from one device to the next, left to right. By default, the Device View displays only a single chain, but there is actually no limit to the number of chains contained within a track.

heading_context.text: 25.1.1 Signal Flow and Parallel Device Chains

blocks.text: Racks allow (among other things) additional device chains to be added to any track. When a track has multiple chains, they operate in parallel: In Instrument and Effect Racks, each chain receives the same input signal at the same time, but then processes its signal serially through its own devices. The output of each of the parallel chains is mixed together, producing the Rack’s output.

blocks.text: One unique property of Racks are their Macro Controls.

blocks.text: The Macro Controls are a bank of knobs, each capable of addressing any number of parameters from any devices in a Rack. How you use them is up to you — whether it be for convenience, by making an important device parameter more accessible; for defining exotic, multi-parameter morphs of rhythm and timbre; or for constructing a mega-synth, and hiding it away behind a single customized interface. See Using the Macro Controls for a detailed explanation of how to do this.

blocks.text: 25.5 Zones
blocks.raw_html: 25.5 Zones

blocks.text: Zones are sets of data filters that reside at the input of every chain in an Instrument or Effect Rack. Together, they determine the range of values that can pass through to the device chain. By default, zones behave transparently, never requiring your attention. They can be reconfigured, however, to form sophisticated control setups. The three types of zones, whose editors are toggled with the buttons above the Chain List, are Key, Velocity, and Chain Select. The adjacent Hide button whisks them out of sight.

blocks.raw_html: 25.5.1 Signal Flow through Zones

blocks.text: To understand how zones work, let’s examine the signal flow in a MIDI Effect Rack. Our MIDI Effect Rack resides in the device chain of a MIDI track, and therefore processes MIDI signals. We will assume that it contains four parallel device chains, each containing one MIDI effect.

blocks.text: All MIDI data in the track is passed to its device chain, and therefore into the input of the MIDI Effect Rack.

blocks.text: Our MIDI Effect Rack has four device chains, all of which receive the same MIDI data at the same time.
blocks.raw_html: • Our MIDI Effect Rack has four device chains, all of which receive the same MIDI data at the same time.

blocks.text: Before any MIDI data can enter a device chain, it must be able to pass through every zone in that chain. Every chain in a MIDI Effect Rack has three zones: a key zone, a velocity zone and a chain select zone.
blocks.raw_html: • Before any MIDI data can enter a device chain, it must be able to pass through every zone in that chain. Every chain in a MIDI Effect Rack has three zones: a key zone, a velocity zone and a chain select zone.

blocks.text: An incoming MIDI note gets compared to a chain’s key zone. If the MIDI note lies within the key zone, it is passed to the next zone for comparison; if it does not, then we already know that the note will not be passed to that chain’s devices.

blocks.text: The same comparisons are made for the chain’s velocity and chain select zones. If a note also lies within both of these zones, then it is passed to the input of the first device in that chain.

blocks.text: In MIDI Effect Racks, fade ranges attenuate the velocities of notes entering a chain. In Instrument Racks and Audio Effect Racks, which both output audio signals, fade ranges attenuate the volume level at each chain’s output. So what happens, then, if the Chain selector is moved outside of the chain select zone where a sound is currently playing? If the zone ends in a fade range, the chain’s output volume is attenuated to zero while the Chain selector is outside of the zone. If the zone had no fade range, the output volume is not attenuated, allowing the chain’s effects (like long reverb tails or delays) to fade out according to their own settings.

blocks.text: 25.6 Drum Racks
blocks.raw_html: 25.6 Drum Racks

blocks.text: We’ve already talked a bit about Drum Racks, and most of their features are the same as those found in Instrument and Effect Racks. But Drum Racks have a slightly different layout, some unique controls and special behavior that is optimized for creating drum kits.
blocks.raw_html: We’ve already talked a bit about Drum Racks, and most of their features are the same as those found in Instrument and Effect Racks. But Drum Racks have a slightly different layout, some unique controls and special behavior that is optimized for creating drum kits.

blocks.text: In addition to the standard selectors found on all Racks, Drum Racks have four additional controls in the view column. From top to bottom, these are toggles for the Input/Output, Send, and Return sections, and the Auto Select button.

blocks.text: Input/Output Section - The Receive chooser sets the incoming MIDI note to which the drum chain will respond. The list shows note names, MIDI note numbers and standard GM drum equivalents. The Play slider sets the outgoing MIDI note that will be sent to the devices in the chain. The Choke chooser allows you to set a chain to one of sixteen choke groups. Any chains that are in the same choke group will silence the others when triggered. This is useful for choking open hihats by triggering closed ones, for example. If “All Notes“ is selected in the Receive chooser, the Play and Choke choosers are disabled — in this case, the chain simply passes the note that it receives to its devices. The small Preview button to the left of these choosers fires a note into the chain, making it easy to check your mappings away from a MIDI controller.

Note that send controls are not available until return chains have been created.

blocks.text: 25.6.1 Pad View
blocks.raw_html: 25.6.1 Pad View

blocks.text: The Pad View is unique to Drum Racks and offers an easy way to map and manipulate samples and devices. Each pad represents one of the 128 available MIDI notes. The pad overview to the left shifts the set of visible pads up or down in groups of 16, either by dragging the view selector to a new area or by using your computer keyboard’s up and down arrow keys. Use the Alt (Win) / Cmd (Mac) modifier to shift the view by single rows instead.
blocks.raw_html: The Pad View is unique to Drum Racks and offers an easy way to map and manipulate samples and devices. Each pad represents one of the 128 available MIDI notes. The pad overview to the left shifts the set of visible pads up or down in groups of 16, either by dragging the view selector to a new area or by using your computer keyboard’s up and down arrow keys. Use the Alt (Win) / Cmd (Mac) modifier to shift the view by single rows instead.

blocks.text: Almost any object from Live’s browser — samples, effects, instruments and presets — can be dragged onto a pad, mapping automatically to the pad’s note and creating or reconfiguring internal chains and devices as necessary. Dropping a sample onto an empty pad, for example, creates a new chain containing a Simpler, with the dropped sample ready to play from the pad’s note. If you then drag an audio effect to the same pad, it is placed downstream from the Simpler in the same chain. To replace the Simpler, simply drop another sample onto the same pad — any downstream audio effects or upstream MIDI effects will be left intact and only the Simpler and sample will be replaced.

blocks.text: In addition to dragging objects from the browser, pads can also be filled quickly via Hot-Swap. If you’re in Hot-Swap mode, pressing the D key will toggle the Hot-Swap target between the Drum Rack itself and the last selected pad.

You can also use these variations or create builds and drops, or make instant jumps between different Macro Control settings while recording or performing.

blocks.text: 25.8 Mixing With Racks
blocks.raw_html: 25.8 Mixing With Racks

blocks.text: Any Instrument or Drum Rack that contains more than one chain can be viewed and mixed alongside the tracks in the Session View’s mixer. A track that contains these Racks will have a button in its title bar, which will fold the Rack’s mixer in or out. Likewise, any nested chains within the Rack will also have this button. This makes it easy to get an overview of your Rack’s hierarchy — or hide it when you just want to work on your mix.

A track that contains these Racks will have a button in its title bar, which will fold the Rack’s mixer in or out. Likewise, any nested chains within the Rack will also have this button. This makes it easy to get an overview of your Rack’s hierarchy — or hide it when you just want to work on your mix.

blocks.text: Chains in the Session View mixer look similar to tracks, but they have no clip slots. Their mixing and routing controls mirror those found in the Rack’s chain list, so any changes made to these controls in either area will be reflected in the other immediately. Likewise, many chain operations such as reordering, renaming and regrouping can be performed from either the mixer or the chain list. Clicking in a chain’s mixer title bar shows only that chain’s devices in the Device View.

blocks.text: 25.8.1 Extracting Chains
blocks.raw_html: 25.8.1 Extracting Chains

blocks.text: All chains can be dragged from their parent Racks and placed into other tracks or Racks, either from the chain list or from the Session View mixer. A Drum Rack’s return chains can also be extracted, and will create new return tracks if dragged to the mixer. Drum chains have an additional feature: when dragged from the mixer to a new track, they take their MIDI notes with them. For example, if you are working on a MIDI drum loop within a single track and decide that you would like to move just the snare onto its own track, simply select the snare chain’s title bar in the mixer and drag it to the mixer’s drop area. This creates a new track with the full contents of the snare chain: both its devices and its MIDI data. If you would like to extract only the devices, drag from the chain list instead of from the mixer.

owner_requirements.title: installed vocabulary and examples
owner_requirements.contract:
**D-installed / E3–E5.** The installed schema declares Audio Effect, MIDI Effect,
Instrument and Drum rack classes. Each declares sixteen macro control fields,
visibility count, randomization and snapshot exclusions, a chain list and macro
variations. ZoneRange declares minimum, maximum and two crossfade bounds;
MacroSnapshot declares sixteen values and sixteen presence flags. The retained
Suite demo contains respectively 23, 1, 8 and 1 rack occurrences. The retained
slicing preset contains five snapshots. These are documentary assertions, not
load/save or semantic rules for the private field names. In particular the Drum
branch's stored selector range does **not** establish a Drum Rack zone editor.

owner_requirements.title: rack type and legal signal placement
owner_requirements.contract:
**D12 / E1 §25.2.** MIDI Effect Racks hold MIDI effects on MIDI tracks. Audio Effect
Racks hold audio effects on audio paths, including after an instrument on a MIDI
track. Instrument and Drum chains order MIDI effects before an instrument and
audio effects after it. Invalid placement is outside the documented valid
configuration; exact drag rejection, relocation, replacement and malformed-file
responses are U. This does not resolve the file-reader question in
REQ-LIVE-SET-STRUCTURE-012.

owner_requirements.title: serial, parallel and nested flow
owner_requirements.contract:
**D12 / E1 §25.1.1.** Devices within a chain process left to right. Instrument and
effect rack chains receive the same input in parallel subject to their zones;
their outputs combine at the rack output, then feed downstream devices. Drum
chains receive assigned notes instead (REQ-016). A rack may contain racks and
acts as a device in the enclosing chain. Exact summation, ordering of coincident
MIDI events, latency and maximum practical nesting depth are U.

owner_requirements.title: creation, grouping and dismantling
owner_requirements.contract:
**D12 / E1 §25.2.** Loading a generic rack creates an empty rack. Group selected
devices, Group to Drum Rack and grouping existing chains create enclosing racks;
repeated grouping can nest them. Selecting a rack title and Ungroup dismantles
that rack. The manual does not define flattening/routing resolution for every
multi-chain or return-containing rack; those outcomes are U.

owner_requirements.title: chain list and selection
owner_requirements.contract:
**D12 / E1 §§25.3–25.4.1.** Dropping devices, presets or chains in the chain-list
drop area adds chains. Selecting a chain shows its devices; multiple selections
show their count. Chains expose activator, solo and hot-swap; audio-output rack
chains also expose volume/pan. Rack-title selection addresses the whole rack for
move/copy/delete. Auto Select selects chains currently processing signals;
Drum Rack selection follows receipt of the assigned note. Exact solo/activator
audio interaction, selection expiry and contention with manual selection are U.

owner_requirements.title: available zone filters
owner_requirements.contract:
**D12 / E1 §§25.5–25.5.1.** Instrument and MIDI Effect Racks have key, velocity and
selector zones; a note enters a chain only if it passes all three. Audio Effect
Racks have selector zones, without MIDI key/velocity zones. Drum Racks have no
zone editor; their Receive choosers filter notes. All matching parallel chains
can receive the same qualifying input.

owner_requirements.title: zone editing and ranges
owner_requirements.contract:
**D12 / E1 §§25.5–25.5.4.1.** Zones can be moved and resized, with separately
editable fades. Key zones cover selected MIDI keys; velocity zones use Note On
velocities 1–127. The selector scale is 0–127; the documented initial selector
zone is the single value 0. Multiple chains may share ranges. Exact rounding,
edge inclusion for resized ranges, out-of-range edits and MIDI velocity-zero
interpretation are U here; note encoding belongs to [MIDI note storage](midi-note-storage.md).

owner_requirements.title: fade destination
owner_requirements.contract:
**D12 / E1 §§25.5.2–25.5.4.** Key/velocity fades attenuate incoming note velocity.
Selector fades in a MIDI Effect Rack attenuate note velocity. Selector fades in
Instrument and Audio Effect Racks attenuate chain output audio. Exact fade law,
rounding to MIDI velocity, overlap normalization and treatment of a zero-length
fade are U; no linear or equal-power equation is specified.

owner_requirements.title: selector filtering of controllers
owner_requirements.contract:
**D12 / E1 §25.5.4.** Instrument and MIDI Effect Rack selector zones filter notes
by default, allowing other MIDI events such as controllers through. Enabling
Chain Selector Filters MIDI Ctrl makes the selector filter all MIDI events.
Held-note release routing and sustain/channel-mode edge cases remain U.

owner_requirements.title: selector movement and existing tails
owner_requirements.contract:
**D12 / E1 §25.5.4.** For an audio-output chain with a fade ending its selector
zone, moving outside attenuates the output to zero. With no fade, leaving the
selector zone does not attenuate existing output; an existing effect tail may
finish according to that effect. This distinction does not specify audio effect
input admission, voice lifetime, clicks, smoothing or compensation changes.

owner_requirements.title: macro count and visibility
owner_requirements.contract:
**D12 / E1 §25.7; E2 §§23.2.3,23.2.6.1.** A rack supports up to sixteen macros;
a newly created factory rack, with no custom default or loaded preset, shows
eight. Visibility controls change the number shown; shown/hidden state is
saved with the Set. Hidden-control mapping activity and lower visibility bound
are U. E3 corroborates sixteen storage slots, without proving runtime limits.

owner_requirements.title: mapping and ranges
owner_requirements.contract:
**D12 / E1 §25.7.1.** Entering Macro Map Mode highlights mappable controls, shows
macro Map buttons and opens the Mapping Browser. Select a contained parameter,
then a macro's Map button to create an assignment; one macro can address several
parameters. Min/Max refine each assignment; Min greater than Max inverts it,
and Invert Range reverses the current range. Assignments can be edited/deleted
in that browser; leaving Map Mode ends this editing mode. Exact interpolation,
quantized parameters and out-of-domain mappings are U.

owner_requirements.title: delegated control and macro display
owner_requirements.contract:
**D12 / E1 §25.7.1.** A mapped device parameter is disabled for direct control;
clip-envelope modulation remains possible. A single mapping supplies its name
and units to the macro by default. Multiple mappings restore the generic macro
name regardless of whether their units match, absent a separately applied
custom name. Multiple mappings use 0–127 units unless every target has the same
unit type and range; in that case, the common units and range are retained.
Custom names/colors/info text are editable. Restored values after unmapping and
interactions with automation override are U.

owner_requirements.title: randomization and exclusions
owner_requirements.contract:
**D12 / E1 §25.7.2.** Rand randomizes mapped macros. Exclude Macro from
Randomization preserves an excluded mapped control. Macros assigned to Volume
parameters in unmodified factory Instrument Rack presets, without a user
exclusion override, are excluded by default. This last clause
does not assert an automatic exclusion after every new volume mapping.
Distribution, seed, correlation, repeatability, unchanged-value probability,
hidden/unmapped controls and randomization undo granularity are U.

owner_requirements.title: variations
owner_requirements.contract:
**D12 / E1 §25.7.3.** New stores current macro state as a variation, initially
named sequentially Variation 1, Variation 2, and so on. Variations can be
renamed, duplicated and deleted. Launch recalls a stored state; Overwrite
replaces it with the current state. Exclude Macro From Variations prevents that
control changing on launch; disabling the exclusion restores participation.
Snapshot behavior during mapping changes, which unmapped values are present,
parameter automation ownership, launch scheduling and interpolation are U.

owner_requirements.title: drum receive, play and choke
owner_requirements.contract:
**D12 / E1 §25.6.** Receive selects the note triggering a drum chain; Play selects
the outgoing note delivered to its devices. Chains assigned the same one of
sixteen choke groups silence one another when triggered. Receive All Notes
disables Play/Choke and passes through the received note. Preview fires a note
into a chain. Choke release envelopes, exact stop time, same-sample arbitration,
self-choke and preview velocity are U.

owner_requirements.title: drum sends and returns
owner_requirements.contract:
**D12 / E1 §§25.2,25.6.** Drum Racks have up to six audio-effect return chains.
Drum-chain sends feed them after the drum chain's fader; send controls require
at least one return chain. Each return's Audio To can target the rack output or
a Set return track. A seventh return's UI/error behavior, return feedback,
missing destinations, send scaling and compensation are U.

owner_requirements.title: dropping onto pads
owner_requirements.contract:
**D12 / E1 §25.6.1.** Each pad denotes a MIDI note. With factory dropping defaults,
a sample on an empty pad creates a chain with Simpler. Dropping an audio effect
on that pad adds it after the instrument. A replacement sample replaces the
Simpler/sample and preserves upstream MIDI and downstream audio effects.
Custom dropping defaults are outside this clause; failed-load atomicity is U.

owner_requirements.title: pad distribution, swapping and layering
owner_requirements.contract:
**D12 / E1 §25.6.1.** Multiple samples dropped normally populate chromatically
upward from the destination, replacing samples while preserving effects.
Alt-drag on Windows / Cmd-drag on macOS layers them in a nested Instrument Rack.
Dragging a pad to another swaps note assignments; existing clips keep their
notes and therefore address the new sounds. The same platform modifier layers
both pads' chains in a nested Instrument Rack. Overflow above note 127, sample
ordering within a multiselection and effects during failed loads are U.

owner_requirements.title: pads represent notes, including multiple chains
owner_requirements.contract:
**D12 / E1 §25.6.1.** The 128-note pad map shows groups of sixteen. Changing Receive
updates pad presentation; matching chains, including nested ones, respond to
the note. A one-chain pad shows that chain's name and permits rename/hot-swap.
A multiple-chain pad displays Multi; mute/solo/preview address all its chains,
rename/hot-swap are disabled, and delete removes all those chains. Exact mixed
mute/solo icon semantics and controller scrolling protocols are U.

owner_requirements.title: rack mixing in Session
owner_requirements.contract:
**D12 / E1 §25.8.** Instrument/Drum racks with multiple chains can unfold into the
Session mixer. Chains have no clip slots. Their controls mirror the rack list;
selecting a chain's mixer title shows its devices. Multiselected Session chains
share a mixer parameter adjustment; the same adjustment from the rack chain
list does not invoke this multi-chain behavior. Relative scaling/clamping of
unequal starting values is U.

owner_requirements.title: extracting chains
owner_requirements.contract:
**D12 / E1 §25.8.1.** Chains can be moved to other racks/tracks. Dragging a drum
chain from the Session mixer to a new track transfers its devices and MIDI
notes. Dragging from the chain list transfers devices only. Dragging a drum
return to the mixer creates a return track. The exact treatment of shared-note
chains, nested mappings, clip ownership, automation, sends and source empty
clips is U; no broad preservation/undo promise is implied.

owner_requirements.title: inserting common devices
owner_requirements.contract:
**D12 / E2 §§23,23.2.** Double-clicking a browser device targets the selected track
or creates a track if none is selected. Enter loads a selected device/preset on
a selected destination track. Devices can be dragged into track/device views;
sample drop on an empty MIDI Device View creates Simpler. Chains follow MIDI
effects → instrument → audio effects and process left to right. Exact
insertion position with existing selection and incompatible-device handling
are U beyond the explicit paste rule below.

owner_requirements.title: move, remove and paste
owner_requirements.contract:
**D12 / E2 §23.2.** Device title selection and Delete/Backspace removes the device;
dragging its title reorders or moves it between tracks. Cut/copy/paste/duplicate
apply to devices. Paste inserts before the selected device; selecting the empty
space after the last device permits paste at the end. Rack title selection
addresses its whole contents (REQ-005). No audio continuity or retained-tail
guarantee follows from the manual's qualified continuity statement.

owner_requirements.title: activator bypass
owner_requirements.contract:
**D12 / E2 §23.2.1.** The activator turns a device on/off; the manual describes an
off device as leaving the signal unprocessed. For an audio effect this provides
a qualitative bypass requirement. It does not establish sample equality,
latency changes, tail retention, CPU counters, retained processor state or the
meaning of unprocessed MIDI at a disabled instrument's audio output; those
outcomes remain U.

owner_requirements.title: presets and hot-swap
owner_requirements.contract:
**D12 / E2 §§23.2.3–23.2.5.** Devices/racks can save settings as presets. Save Preset
opens the browser with a prospective name; Enter confirms and Esc cancels the
save process. Dragging a device title into a Places folder is another save
route. Hot-Swap connects a target with the browser, and only compatible device
types can be swapped. Q, Esc or the close controls exit Hot-Swap; exit alone is
not documented as restoring an earlier loaded preset. Overwrite/cancel disk
atomicity, media collection, failed loads and custom-default precedence require
separate evidence. Current-manual A/B device states and newer defaults are not
silently included in this bounded contract.

owner_requirements.title: malformed state, cancellation and teardown
owner_requirements.contract:
**U / E1–E5 limits.** For malformed zone bounds, illegal note/choke/return values,
missing/duplicate snapshot members, cancelled pad/extract/mapping operations,
held notes while deleting/unmapping/choking, lost media or closing during load,
no rack-specific refusal, repair, rollback, cleanup or timing outcome has been
established. Generic file parsing remains owned by the container/structure
specifications; their checks do not prove rack-specific semantic validation.
